result.summary: Phineus finishes advising the Argonauts, and after the Harpies are driven off they pass the Clashing Rocks with Athena's help. They sail on, meet Apollo at dawn, are feasted by King Lycus, and lose the seer Idmon to a boar.

scenes.title: Phineus's house and Paraebius
scenes.summary: The Boreads return from chasing the Harpies. Phineus tells of Paraebius's inherited curse, and sacrifice and feast follow.
scenes.stakes: Phineus remains blind and afflicted, and the Argonauts need his guidance for the voyage.

scenes.title: Tale of Cyrene and Aristaeus
scenes.summary: The narrator explains the Etesian winds through Aristaeus, son of Apollo and Cyrene, who ended a plague on Ceos.
scenes.stakes: The people of the Minoan Isles are threatened by plague from the scorching Dog-star.

scenes.title: Passing the Clashing Rocks
scenes.summary: The Argonauts release a dove, row through the Clashing Rocks, and Athena pushes Argo through. Tiphys rejoices at their escape.
scenes.stakes: The crew risk being crushed between the rocks.

place.name: Cyanean rocks
place.modern_name: Bosporus entrance to the Black Sea

scenes.title: Jason's fear and Apollo's isle
scenes.summary: Jason confesses his fear and is cheered. They sail along the Bithynian coast and see Apollo at dawn on Thynias, where they sacrifice.
scenes.stakes: Jason fears failing to bring his comrades home; the crew need the god's favour.

scenes.title: Feast with Lycus
scenes.summary: At the Acherusian headland, Lycus welcomes the heroes, hears their tale and praises Heracles. He offers his son Dascylus as guide.
scenes.stakes: Lycus's land is being eaten away by the Bebrycians.

place.name: Acherusian headland, land of the Mariandyni

scenes.title: Death of Idmon
scenes.summary: A boar kills the seer Idmon. The heroes bury him and the narrator mentions his tomb and a later cult.
scenes.stakes: Idmon is doomed to die despite his prophetic skill.

alias_notes.explanation: The text spells the same man both ways.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable simile comparing Athena's swift descent to a traveller's thought racing home.
Vivid simile of the rowers as straining ploughing oxen.

analysis.text: Divine aid and fate shape the voyage: Phineus's prophecy, Athena's push and Apollo's epiphany guide the heroes, while Idmon's death shows prophecy cannot defeat fate.
The digressions on Cyrene and Aristaeus, Megarian Soonautes and Idmon's cult explain real cults and place-names, reflecting Hellenistic interest in aetiology and colonial claims.

legacy.text: The Clashing Rocks, passed by a bird test, influenced later tellings of the Symplegades and similar moving-rock motifs in literature.

fun_facts.text: Apollonius, the poet, worked as librarian at Alexandria, and his aetiological digressions reflect scholarly interest in cult origins.

language_notes.text: Aea is the land of Aeetes, the Argonauts' goal, where the Golden Fleece lies; the 'deadly rocks' are the Clashing Rocks they must pass.
The Cyprian goddess is Aphrodite (Venus), associated with Cyprus. Phineus tells them her help, through love, will decide the outcome of the quest for the fleece.
The Dictaean cliff is on Crete, named for Mount Dicte. The Harpies, winged storm-spirits, are spared because Iris, the goddess, pledged they would not trouble Phineus again.
Aceres appears to be a form of Aeetes' name or city; the seer foretold the Argonauts' arrival, linking to his prophetic power.
A Hamadryad is a tree nymph whose life is bound to a particular tree and who dies when it is felled.
'Health' here is almost certainly a mistranslation or misprint for 'hearth', the altar-fire where the sacrifice is burned.
Etesian winds are the steady northerly summer winds of the Aegean, whose name means 'yearly'.
'The Far-Darter' is a standard epithet for Apollo, the archer god; the 'Minoan Isles' are the Aegean islands near Crete, including Ceos.
The Dog-star is Sirius, whose rising in late summer was associated with scorching heat and disease.
'Welkin' is an archaic word for the sky or heavens.
'The tide returning' means the surge of water flowing back as the rocks close again, dragging the ship toward them.
The ship leaps back twice as far as the rowers advance, showing how the current opposes them.
'Hest' is an archaic word for command; the king is Pelias, who sent Jason on this quest.
"Torn limb from limb" and "yea" are archaic emphasis: Jason says he should have refused Pelias even at the cost of a cruel death.
"Thou talkest at thine ease, eating only for thine own life" means Tiphys speaks untroubled, since he worries only about himself. "Not a whit" means "not at all"; Jason's words are ironic.
"I trow" is archaic for "I believe" or "I am confident." The "striking rocks" are the Clashing Rocks (Symplegades) the Argo has just passed.
"The son of Athamas" is Phrixus, who fled Orchomenus on the golden ram; the Argonauts are heading for its fleece in Colchis.
The Hyperboreans were a legendary people dwelling far north, whom Apollo was said to visit; Lycia was one of his chief homes.
"Haemonian land" is Thessaly, the Argonauts' homeland. "Of the Dawn" renders the cult title Eoios, tied to the god's dawn appearance.
"Propitiate" means to win the favour of; "libations" are liquid offerings poured out to a god.
Apollo's killing of the serpent at Parnassus (called Delphyne here) is the myth of Delphi's founding. The cry "Ie Paieon" gives "Healer" in the refrain.
Soonautes means roughly 'saviour of sailors' in Greek; the name is explained in the next sentence by the river's rescue of the Megarians' ships.
"Behests" means commands or orders; here, the tasks Pelias imposed on Jason.
"Ye cleave your long path" is archaic: you plough your way through the sea. "Ye" is the plural "you".
"I trow" is archaic for "I believe". "The son of Tyndareus" is Polydeuces, here named by his mortal foster father.
"Hied" means hurried.
"Fell" here is an old word for a stretch of wild upland or moor.
The narrator says Apollo ordered the colonists to honour Idmon as city hero, but they later honoured Agamestor instead, an aetiological comment on local cult.

context_notes.text: Zetes and Calais, winged sons of the north wind Boreas, had been sent to chase away the Harpies that fouled Phineus' food.
Phineus is a blind seer, punished by the gods for revealing too much of the future, and tormented by the Harpies.
Atoning sacrifices at an altar were the usual Greek way to appease an offended divinity and lift an inherited curse.
Haemonia is an old name for Thessaly. Apollo takes Cyrene to Libya, where the city Cyrene was later founded.
The 'blessed twelve' are the twelve Olympian gods. The dove is a test: if it passes the rocks, the ship may attempt the passage.
Athena is the Argonauts' divine protector, and she helps them here.
The Clashing Rocks were fated to stop moving once a ship passed through them safely, so they stay fixed afterwards.
Pelias, king of Iolcus, sent Jason on this quest, hoping he would not return.
The son of Leto is Apollo, god of archery, music, prophecy and healing; his twin is Artemis.
Wrapping thigh bones in fat and burning them was the standard Greek sacrifice, with the meat eaten afterward.
Concord (Homonoia) was worshipped as a goddess; the temple marks the crew's oath of unity, a founding story typical of epic.
The cave was believed to be an entrance to the Underworld, ruled by Hades; the Acherusian headland was associated with the descent of Heracles to fetch Cerberus.
Polydeuces had just killed Amycus, king of the Bebrycians, in a boxing match, which explains the welcome.
Heracles' journey to fetch the girdle of Hippolyte, queen of the Amazons, was one of his Labours.
The sons of Tyndareus are the twins Castor and Polydeuces, honoured as divine; Lycus promises them temple worship.
Idmon was a seer among the Argonauts and had foreseen his own death on this voyage but joined anyway.

literary_notes.text: Phineus' wish for death shows his weariness and faith in a blessed afterlife, deepening his portrait as a suffering but pious seer.
The repeated 'more and more' and 'day after day' stress the endless, escalating misery of Paraebius, making his suffering feel inescapable.
The nymph's own death becomes the curse: the felled tree's loss is repaid as lasting suffering for the guilty man's family.
Athena's swift descent is compared to a traveller's mind racing home across land and sea, conveying the speed of thought.
The ship is compared to a cylinder, a roller, as it runs over the wave, giving a vivid image of its motion.
Likening Argo to a winged arrow stresses the speed of her passage once the goddess pushes her through.
Being 'saved from Hades' treats the escape as a return from death, conveying how near destruction was.
Jason's confession is partly a test of his men, showing a leader who is anxious yet calculating.
The rowers are compared to sweating ploughing oxen, conveying their exhaustion through a homely farm image.
The faint twilight is described precisely, setting a threshold mood before the god appears.
Golden locks, silver bow and the quaking island make Apollo's epiphany dazzling and awe-inspiring.
Orpheus addresses the departed god directly, turning narration into prayer.
Vivid sight and sound, with cliffs, thundering waves and plane trees, builds a grim yet grand setting for the entrance to the Underworld.
The seer who knows the future cannot escape his own fate, underscoring the power of necessity.
The boar is described as a hidden, dreaded monster, making the sudden attack seem inevitable and fated.
The narrator points to a landmark visible in his own day, linking myth to present reality and lending authority.
The narrator steps forward, invoking the Muses and reluctantly telling the tale, a signature of Apollonius' personal storytelling voice.
